lesson.title: The List Toolkit: An Overview of Built-in Methods
lesson.summary: What a method actually is, and a first look at the family of built-in list methods, including the crucial distinction between ones that return None and ones that return a value.
lesson.body:
Because lists are mutable, Python gives them an entire toolkit of built-in operations for changing their contents, called methods. A method is a function that belongs to an object and is called using dot notation directly on that object, which is different from a regular built-in function like len(my_list), where the list is passed in as an argument. When you write my_list.append(5), you are asking the list object itself, the one stored in my_list, to run its own append operation, rather than passing my_list into some separate append function.

List methods generally fall into a few families based on what they do. Some add elements: append puts one item on the end, insert places one item at a specific position. Some remove elements: remove deletes the first match of a given value, pop deletes an item at a position and hands it back to you, clear empties the whole list. Some reorder the list: sort arranges elements from smallest to largest by default, reverse flips the order entirely. And some just answer questions about the list without changing it: count tells you how many times a value appears, index tells you where a value first shows up. The next several concepts in this unit walk through append, insert, remove, pop, and sort individually, in depth, but seeing them grouped this way now should make each one feel like a specific case of a pattern you already recognize rather than an unrelated new fact to memorize.

The single most important thing to internalize before going further is this: many list methods mutate the list in place and return None, while a smaller number return something useful. append, insert, remove, and sort all belong to the first group, silently modifying the original list object and giving back nothing at all. pop is the standout exception, since its entire purpose is handing back the value it removed.

words = ["pear", "kiwi"]
result = words.append("mango")
print(words)
print(result)

print(words.count("kiwi"))
print(words.index("mango"))

Trace this precisely. words.append("mango") mutates the list in place, so words becomes ["pear", "kiwi", "mango"], but the append call itself evaluates to None, so result is assigned None. print(words) shows ['pear', 'kiwi', 'mango'], and print(result) shows None on its own line. words.count("kiwi") counts how many times "kiwi" appears in the current list, which is once, printing 1. words.index("mango") reports the position where "mango" first appears, which is index 2, printing 2.

This return-value distinction causes one of the most common beginner bugs in all of introductory Python: writing something like words = words.append("mango"), intending to save the updated list, but instead overwriting words with None, since that is exactly what append returns. The list was already updated in place before that assignment ever happened, so the assignment was not only unnecessary, it actively destroyed the variable. Whenever you call a method on a list, pause and ask two questions: does this method change the list in place, and does it hand anything back? Getting those two answers right, for every method you meet from here on, is what this concept is really teaching.
